extracted.intended_audience: architects, clergy, and educated readers interested in ecclesiastical/early Christian architecture and liturgical furnishings
extracted.subtask_description: Design and evaluative principles for early Christian church architecture and furnishings (especially pulpits, seating, ornamentation, mosaics and lighting), illustrated by the Cathedral of Torcello. Emphasizes moral/spiritual expression, functional details for worship, and appropriate ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of humility and refuge in church architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A church built by exiles should express simplicity, tenderness, and shelter rather than ambition or splendor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “a simple and tender effort to recover some of the form of the temples which they had loved, and to do honor to God by that which they were erecting, while distress and humiliation prevented the desire, and prudence precluded the admission, either of luxury of ornament or magnificence of plan.” The building should look like a refuge rather than a monumental display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior restraint with selective decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The exterior should be ‘absolutely devoid of decoration’ except for a few important entrances or elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin notes the exterior is plain except the western entrance and lateral door which have carved sideposts, architrave, and sculptured crosses. Restraint on exterior surfaces directs emphasis to a few meaningful features rather than pervasive ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminousness — admit and diffuse natural light
rubrics_metrics.description: A church should admit sunshine freely so interior details remain visible and the space feels hopeful rather than gloomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “It is remarkable... where the slightest details of the sculptures and mosaics are visible, even when twilight is deepening.” Light is associated with comfort and hope for worshippers, so design should avoid artificial darkness or heavy gloom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of sacred subjects focused on mercy and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Interior imagery (mosaics, decorations) should concentrate on central Christian facts — the mercy of Christ and His coming to judge — rather than worldly, political or trivial subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin contrasts Torcello’s selection (Christ, the Virgin, apostles; Christ coming to judgment) with other churches that mix political events and grotesque subjects. The emphasis should be devotional and hope-inspiring rather than worldly or satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic and inventive ornamentation (vine, serpent, adapted classical forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical motifs may be adapted imaginatively and given Christian symbolism (e.g., vine as Christ, serpent as eternity or subdued Satan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a classical wreathed fillet is turned into a triple-knotted serpent; vine-forms and trefoiled leaves are used and boldly detached to cast changing shadows. Ornament should carry symbolic meaning and vitality rather than being dead repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied and expressive carving of capitals and ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals and carved elements should show individual variation, strong chiselling, and graceful, fanciful designs rather than uniform imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Every one of them is different in design, and their variations are as graceful as they are fanciful.” Detailed execution (sharp penetrations, deep drill holes, lively lines) is praised as effective visual expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic reuse of ornament for surface enrichment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reused carved marbles and fragments may be fitted into new work for surface enrichment even if patterns are arbitrarily cut; this indicates vitality and practical distinction between architectural effect and abstract perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin explains that early builders often took decorated pieces as a dressmaker takes lace — using portions where needed. Careless fitting is not necessarily barbarous but can indicate abundant creative power and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid highly decorated pulpits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulpits ought never to be highly decorated; excessive magnificence can make the speaker appear mean or diminutive and discourage preaching from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I believe, therefore, in the first place, that pulpits ought never to be highly decorated... the speaker is apt to look mean or diminutive if the pulpit is either on a very large scale or covered with splendid ornament.” Very elaborate pulpits often end up unused for important preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit only chaste, grave and noble ornaments; prioritize God’s word over comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ornamentation used on pulpits or church furniture should be chaste, grave and noble and serve to honor God’s word rather than to increase the preacher’s ease or personal display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Whatever ornaments we admit ought clearly to be of a chaste, grave, and noble kind; and what furniture we employ, evidently more for the honoring of God's word than for the ease of the preacher.” Ornamental choices should reflect reverence and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional pulpit form for effective preaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulpit proportions and details should support the preacher’s action and practical needs (e.g., an oval form giving room for full bodily action; a hollowed desk that holds a book securely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin describes the Torcello pulpit as slightly oval to give free room for the action of the entire person, and a desk hollowed into a shallow curve leaving a ledge so a book “settles itself there... without the least chance of slipping.” Functionality is integral to design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of pulpit decoration to maintain focus on message
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration should not distract from the sermon; if the sermon is regarded as a Divine message, the setting must encourage reverent, undistracted hearing — prefer simple forms even when ornament is lovely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues that when the preacher is seen as sent with a message, people will look with changed eyes upon “that frippery of gay furniture” and desire simple, rock-like places from which the message is delivered. Simplicity heightens the perceived gravity of the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity through austerity in episcopal seating
rubrics_metrics.description: Raised seats and an episcopal throne gain dignity from their severe, unindulgent, and marble character rather than from comfort or elaborate canopies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The marble seats and throne at Torcello (hard, arm-less central throne for distinction) show authority and impressiveness dependent on “the utter absence of any expression either of pride or self-indulgence.” Austerity can be more impressive than ornamented comfort.
